title: Establish SDK transport fanout profiles and per-request deadline heuristics
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Problem statement:
Customers building low-latency, high-throughput features across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs are seeing uneven behavior when requests fan out to multiple model backends, stream responses, or when connection pools are saturated. Symptoms reported: sporadic long tail latencies, inefficient socket reuse, requests waiting on overloaded worker lanes, and confusing retry semantics for streamed responses.

Goal:
Define a cross-SDK transport configuration and recommended runtime profiles that make per-request deadlines deterministic, improve socket reuse/keepalive behavior under fanout, and provide consistent streaming ergonomics (graceful reconnects, partial-result retries, and backpressure-friendly chunking). Deliver language-specific examples (Python/TS/Go), automated tests, telemetry, and a staged rollout plan.

Scope and deliverables:
- Design and implement a set of "fanout profiles" (low-latency, balanced, cost-optimized) that encapsulate: connect/idle/keepalive, pool size and max concurrent requests per connection, per-request deadline defaults, streaming chunk timeouts, and hedging/early-retry windows.
- Standardize per-request deadline API surface across SDKs (deadline vs. timeout distinction) and document best practices for long-polling and streaming workloads.
- Implement adaptive pool priming and TCP_REUSE heuristics to reduce cold-starts under sudden fanout.
- Add cross-sdk integration tests simulating 10x fanout and variable backend tail latencies.
- Telemetry: expose metrics for socket churn, queue wait times, per-request deadline misses, hedged requests, and streaming reconnect rate.
- Migration guide and example configs for customers with Dedicated / Private deployments.

Proposed approach and rationale:
1) Profiles: provide three canonical profiles with clear intended trade-offs:
   - "latency": small per-connection concurrency (1-2), low pooling, short connect/idle timeouts, aggressive keepalive to detect dead peers quickly. Good for conversational, latency-sensitive routes.
   - "balanced": moderate per-connection concurrency (4-8), medium pool size, moderate keepalive. Default for general-purpose generation.
   - "throughput": high per-connection concurrency (16+), larger pools, longer idle/keepalive to amortize connection cost. Good for batch embeddings/reranking.
Rationale: bundling these into named profiles reduces cognitive overhead for integrators and makes it easier to map routing policies to expected SLOs.

2) Deadline semantics: clarify and implement two concepts: "deadline" (absolute time by which request must finish) and "idle-chunk-timeout" (per-chunk streaming inactivity). SDKs must offer both and surface clear priority: deadline preempts chunk timeouts.

3) Hedging and early retry: for high-value requests in "latency" profile, enable optional hedging window (e.g., spawn a second attempt after 60% of expected p50). Ensure idempotency markers and server-side dedup semantics are part of contract.

4) Socket hygiene: adopt a conservative TCP_REUSE policy with connection priming (1-2 warm requests per new socket) and a slow-reap policy for high-throughput pools to avoid thrash under load spikes.

5) Streaming ergonomics: introduce a "stream-resume" helper that attempts N reconnects with a short CRDT-style offset negotiation when server supports it; otherwise provide a best-effort partial-result callback and clear guidance in docs.

Language examples (short extracts):
- Python (requests-style):
  client.request(..., deadline=2.0, profile="latency")
- TypeScript (node):
  await client.generate({ input, timeout: { deadlineMs: 1500, chunkIdleMs: 200 }, profile: 'balanced' })
- Go:
  ctx, cancel := context.WithDeadline(ctx, time.Now().Add(1600*time.Millisecond))
  defer cancel()
  client.Generate(ctx, opts.WithProfile("throughput"))

Acceptance criteria:
- Profiles implemented in all three SDKs and covered by unit + integration tests.
- Perf test showing 30-50% reduction in socket churn under simulated fanout for "balanced" profile.
- Deadline and chunk timeout behavior documented and validated by tests that assert deterministic request cancellation.
- Streaming reconnect helper implemented in at least Python + TS with fallback docs for Go.
- Telemetry emitted and visible in an internal dashboard for the canary namespace.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Aggressive keepalive / short idle timeouts reduce long-tail detection but increase socket churn; balanced defaults are conservative.
- Hedging increases upstream load and must be gated behind customer opt-in or only enabled for small percentage of production traffic at first.
- Stream resume requires protocol support from some backends; provide graceful degradation path.

Rollout plan:
- Week 1: implement profiles and deadline API in Python SDK + unit tests.
- Week 2: port to TypeScript and Go; implement integration harness that simulates backend latency distributions.
- Week 3: internal canary for non-critical routes; monitor telemetry.
- Week 4: expand canary to selected customers (enterprise) and collect feedback.

Related artifacts and links:
- Design doc: https://docs.redwood.ai/confluence/transport-fanout-profiles (draft)
- PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-python/pull/432, https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-js/pull/217
- Load harness: https://internal.redwood.ai/harness/fanout-sim

Notes for reviewers:
- Pay attention to cross-language API ergonomics and naming consistency (deadline vs timeout).
- Validate that hedging control surfaces are opt-in and observable via telemetry.
acceptance_criteria: Profiles are present in Python/TS/Go with consistent naming and documented defaults.
Integration tests simulate 10x fanout and show socket churn improvement for balanced profile.
Deadline and chunk timeouts cause deterministic cancellations and are covered by unit tests.
Streaming resume helper available for Python and TS and documented fallback for Go.
Telemetry emitted for queue wait time, socket churn, deadline misses, and hedged request rate.
